ai.definition: Organ-on-Chip is a microfabricated device that mimics the structure and function of human organs by integrating multiple cell types within a microscale environment. These devices can simulate the physiological and biochemical functions of living tissues and are used to test drug efficacy, toxicity, and metabolism.
ai.howItWorks: Organ-on-Chip technology involves creating tiny channels and chambers using microfabrication techniques, which are then populated with human cells to form an artificial organ. Fluidic systems mimic blood flow and other physiological processes, allowing for the simulation of organ functions in a controlled environment.
ai.problemSolved: Reduces the reliance on animal testing by providing a more accurate model of human biology for drug development, leading to better predictive outcomes and ethical considerations.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves using microfabrication techniques such as photolithography and soft lithography to create channels and chambers. Cells are then introduced into these structures, often through bioprinting or seeding methods.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the chip layout, fabricating the device, populating it with cells, and integrating microfluidic systems to mimic organ functions. This is typically done in cleanroom environments using semiconductor fabrication techniques.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the precision of microfabrication processes, the cost of cell lines used, and the complexity of integrating multiple organ models into a single device. High-quality materials and specialized equipment also contribute to costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow as it gains acceptance in drug development pipelines, leading to increased investment and standardization.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulatory frameworks for Organ-on-Chip devices. However, they may be subject to existing regulations governing in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDs) or toxicity testing methods.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the complexity of maintaining cell viability over time and ensuring accurate simulation of organ functions. Ethical concerns around the use of human cells and potential limitations in fully replicating complex biological systems also exist.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the early stage of commercialization, but if successful, Organ-on-Chip could significantly reduce development costs and timelines for pharmaceutical companies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may focus on improving the longevity and complexity of organ models, integrating more advanced sensing technologies, and expanding applications beyond drug testing into areas such as personalized medicine and disease modeling.

glossary.def: The process of creating microscale structures using techniques similar to those used in semiconductor manufacturing.
Three-dimensional cell cultures that mimic the structure and function of organs, often used in Organ-on-Chip technology.
The science of controlling very small fluid volumes (typically microliters or less) for analysis or synthesis.

subsystems.name: Microfluidic chip
subsystems.role: a palm-sized device with micrometre-scale channels that houses living cells and perfuses them with nutrient fluid.

subsystems.name: Living tissue module
subsystems.role: the biological core — human cells arranged to mimic a specific organ's function.

subsystems.name: Mechanical stimulation
subsystems.role: reproduces physical forces such as breathing, stretching or fluid shear for organs that need them.

subsystems.name: Fluid handling
subsystems.role: delivers culture medium and drugs at controlled flow rates.

subsystems.name: Sensing and imaging
subsystems.role: measures how the tissue responds to a drug.

subsystems.name: Environmental control
subsystems.role: keeps the chip at body temperature and sterile.

buildSteps.title: Design the chip
buildSteps.detail: Engineers lay out channels and chambers in software, choosing dimensions from tens to hundreds of micrometres to mimic organ architecture.

buildSteps.title: Make the master mould
buildSteps.detail: A silicon wafer is patterned with photoresist and etched to create a relief mould, often using soft lithography.

buildSteps.title: Cast the chip
buildSteps.detail: Liquid polymer (usually PDMS) is poured over the mould, cured, and peeled off, forming a slab with microscopic channels.

buildSteps.title: Bond and assemble
buildSteps.detail: The patterned slab is bonded to a flat layer, often by plasma treatment, to seal the channels; ports are punched for tubing.

buildSteps.title: Culture the cells
buildSteps.detail: Human cells — often induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) differentiated into the desired organ type — are grown in flasks.

buildSteps.title: Seed the chip
buildSteps.detail: Cells are introduced into the chip's chambers, where they attach to an extracellular matrix coating and self-organise.

buildSteps.title: Connect fluidics and mechanics
buildSteps.detail: Pumps, tubing and, for organs like lung or gut, vacuum actuators are attached to apply flow and stretching.

buildSteps.title: Run the experiment
buildSteps.detail: The drug is perfused through the chip at a controlled dose; sensors and microscopes record the tissue's response over days or weeks.

buildSteps.title: Analyse results
buildSteps.detail: Outflow is sampled for biomarkers, and images are analysed to assess toxicity or efficacy.

prerequisites.why: the ability to mould and bond micrometre-scale channels is the foundation of the chip.
iPSCs provide a renewable source of human cells that can become many organ types.
keeping cells alive and functional for weeks in a synthetic environment remains difficult.
a chip must reproduce enough of an organ's behaviour to predict human responses.
measuring subtle changes in living tissue non-destructively is hard.
drugs are approved based on animal and human trials; regulators have not yet qualified chips as replacements.

pathway.milestone: single-organ chips (liver, heart, kidney) used in academic and early pharma research to screen for toxicity
pathway.unlocks: better early filtering of unsafe drug candidates.

pathway.milestone: multi-organ 'body-on-a-chip' systems that link several organs with a common blood-like fluid
pathway.unlocks: seeing how a drug's breakdown in the liver affects the heart or brain.

pathway.milestone: qualification by regulators for specific uses, such as liver toxicity testing
pathway.unlocks: chips becoming accepted evidence in drug applications, reducing animal tests.

pathway.milestone: patient-specific chips made from a person's own cells
pathway.unlocks: personalised drug testing and precision medicine.
